en: Anything on or near the road that could cause danger or force you to change speed or direction.
All indicators flashing together to warn others of a hazard or breakdown.
Warning symbols or plates that show a load’s danger type.
Both indicators flashing together to warn other drivers of a hazard or sudden slowing.
A triangular road sign that warns of a danger or difficult situation ahead on the road.
Short for hazard warning lights: all indicators flashing to warn of danger or a stop.
The padded support behind your head on the seat, often called a headrest.
A lot of blood loss from a wound that needs urgent pressure and help.
Water thrown up by tyres on a wet road, which can reduce visibility.
Moving livestock (such as sheep or cattle) along or across a road.
High-visibility clothing (bright/reflective) that makes a person easier to see, especially in poor light.
The main shopping street in a town or city centre.
A tall vehicle such as a lorry or van that can be strongly affected by side winds.
The top of a hill where your view of the road ahead is often limited.
A person riding a horse on or beside the road; treat them as vulnerable road users.
People riding horses on or beside the road.
A bridge with a sharp rise in the middle that can hide traffic beyond it.
An accident, breakdown, or other unexpected event on the road.
Using your direction indicators to show you intend to turn or change lane.
Flashing lights on a vehicle used to show you intend to turn or change lane.
A policy that can cover costs after an accident, damage, or claim.
A document that proves your vehicle has valid insurance cover.
The rear-view mirror inside the car, usually at the top of the windscreen.
A place where roads meet or cross, such as a T-junction or crossroads.
Places where roads meet or cross; smaller road users can be harder to spot there.
The raised stone or concrete edge between the road and the pavement (US: curb).
Pressing the accelerator hard in an automatic car so it changes to a lower gear for quicker acceleration.
When one or more lanes are temporarily closed, often due to roadworks or an incident.
Painted lines on the road that show where each traffic lane is.
Big trucks that carry freight; often called LGVs in the UK.
Older petrol that contained lead; not used for normal road cars today.
Someone learning to drive, often showing L plates on the vehicle.
In the UK, the lane nearest the left-hand side of the road (kerb side) for normal driving.
A place where a road crosses a railway line, often with barriers and warning lights.
A place where a road crosses a railway line, often with barriers and warning lights.
The official body that issues and manages driving licences (in Great Britain, the DVLA).
The official body that issues and manages driving licences (Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency).
When you cannot see far enough ahead because something blocks your view.
A lane that is open for normal moving traffic (not closed or for emergency use only).
Farm animals such as sheep or cattle that may be on or near the road.
A very lengthy type of road vehicle, such as a lorry, coach, or articulated truck.
Small loose stones on a newly surfaced road that can fly up and damage vehicles.
Large goods vehicles used to carry freight (UK term for trucks).
A large goods vehicle used for carrying cargo (also called a truck).
Planes flying near the ground, often near an airport approach.
Gears with more engine power and less speed, useful on hills.
High-beam headlights that light farther ahead but can dazzle other road users.
A larger, busier road that smaller side roads join onto.
The high-intensity headlight setting (full beam) for dark roads with no oncoming traffic.
The more important road at a junction, which usually has priority.
A route you are required to follow, not just a suggested direction.
A speed limit you must obey by law, often shown in a red circle or on overhead gantry signs.
A controlled driving movement such as reversing, turning, or parking.
Small roadside posts that show distance markers and the direction to the nearest emergency phone.
The heaviest legal weight of a vehicle or trailer including its load (also called MAM).
Excused from a legal requirement for approved medical reasons.
A metric unit of length used on UK height and width restriction signs.
A roadside post or sign showing distance along a route, often in miles.
A small roundabout, often marked by a white painted circle on the road.
A small, low-powered motorcycle that often travels more slowly than cars.
Low-powered two-wheel motor vehicles, lighter and slower than most motorcycles.
Legal cover for using a motor vehicle on public roads, protecting against claims from others at minimum.
Powered road vehicles such as cars, vans, and motorcycles (not bicycles or pedestrians).
A rule that limits or bans motorcycles on that stretch of road.
A person riding a motorcycle; they can be less stable and harder to see than cars.
People riding motorcycles; they can be hidden in blind spots and move up beside you quickly.
A high-speed dual-direction road with controlled access for most traffic, shown by blue signs in the UK.
